1. What this handbook will do for you
AI has crossed a threshold. It's not just autocompleting your sentences anymore — it can run whole
workflows, draft your emails, sort your inbox, write your weekly reports from real data, and follow up
with your customers in your voice. This handbook is the map for making that real in your own work —
no hype, no mystique, just the craft.
A note on the case study. Claude — the AI system built by Anthropic — is the working example
throughout this handbook. It's what I use daily and know deeply. But the underlying principles —
how to prompt well, how to think in projects, how to pick the right model for a task, how to build
automations that don't drift over time — apply to any capable AI system. Where something is
Claude-specific I'll say so. Otherwise, treat what follows as general craft. AI systems will keep
changing; the craft will outlast any of them. 
You don't need to be technical. If you can write an email, you can do everything in this guide.
There is no code. You will type normal sentences into a chat box, and your computer will do work
for you. 
Three promises
By the end of this guide, you will know:
How to talk to Claude so it actually understands what you want — and pushes back when
something's unclear.
How to set up Claude Projects so you don't keep re-explaining the same context over and over.
How to automate seven real workflows — daily email triage, weekly reports, research,
applications, content creation, ads, customer follow-up — using both Chat and Cowork.
How to read this
The first five chapters are the foundation. Don't skip them. They teach you the few skills that make every
scenario in Part 2 work. Once you've read those, jump to whichever scenario in Part 2 fits what you
actually need to do this week. Build that one. Then come back for the next.
Treat this like a recipe book, not a textbook. Don't try to memorize. The goal is to use it, get a result,
and iterate. By month two you'll be inventing your own scenarios.

2. The two ways to use Claude
Claude gives you two modes of working: Chat and Cowork. They look similar and live in the same app.
They do different things. Picking the right one for each task saves you hours of frustration.
Where they live: Both Chat and Cowork are available on the same surfaces — the browser at 
claude.ai , the desktop app for Mac and Windows, and the mobile apps for iOS and Android.
Wherever you open Claude, you'll see a switch between "Chat" and "Cowork" in the message box.
Cowork is included on all paid plans; the free plan gets Chat only. 
Chat mode Cowork mode
How you use it You open a chat and type. Every task
starts with you.
You describe a task and hand it off.
Cowork plans, works, and comes back
with a finished output.
What it can do Answer, write, draft, research, brainstorm,
work through problems with you.
Take on multi-step tasks on its own. Work
across your files and connected apps. Run
on a schedule.
Best for Writing, thinking, one-off questions,
drafting, conversation.
Anything you do regularly. Anything that
should happen on a schedule. Multi-step
work that would take you an hour.
In plain language Like a smart assistant you're talking to. Like a smart assistant you're delegating to.
The simple rule
If you would describe the task as "help me think through this" or "write this one thing" — that's
Chat. If you would describe it as "go do this whole job for me" or "do this every Monday" — that's
Cowork.
An example, the same task done both ways
Imagine you want Claude to summarize your emails every morning and tell you what needs your
attention.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 4

CHAT
You open Claude. You type "summarize my
email from this morning." You read the
answer. It's useful.
Tomorrow morning, you do the same thing
again. And the next day.
Works. But you have to remember every time.
COWORK
You describe the task once and set it to run
every weekday at 7:30 AM.
By the time you sit down with coffee, the
summary is already waiting for you.
You set it up once. It happens forever (until
you turn it off).
Which should you start with?
Chat. Always Chat, for the first week or two. Chat teaches you how to talk to Claude. Once you've found
yourself doing the same kind of prompt three times in a row, that's your signal to move that task into
Cowork.
Where does Cowork actually do the work?
This is where the July 2026 update changed things. Cowork now works two ways:
In the cloud (the newer, default way): tasks run on Anthropic's servers. You can start a job on your
laptop, close your laptop, and it keeps going. You'll see the finished result whether you check on
your phone, your laptop, or your desktop.
On your computer (through the desktop app): needed when the task must touch files on your local
machine or drive your browser. Requires the desktop app open on Mac or Windows.
For most scenarios in this handbook — email triage, weekly reports, research, drafting — cloud is fine.
If you specifically want Claude to open files sitting on your Downloads folder or drive your Chrome
browser, the desktop app has to be running.
You don't have to pick. Cowork figures out which mode fits each task. When it needs your desktop, it'll
tell you. Otherwise it just runs. 
How to access Cowork
1 Open Claude anywhere — claude.ai  in your browser, the desktop app, or the mobile app.
2 Look at the message box. There's a toggle between "Chat" and "Cowork."
3 Switch to Cowork. Describe your task in plain language.
4 Claude proposes a plan. You approve. It runs.

3. How to actually talk to Claude
This is the most important chapter. The single biggest reason people don't get value from AI is they
treat it like a search box. Claude is not Google. Search engines reward short queries. Claude rewards 
context.
The recipe for any good prompt
Almost every successful prompt has these four parts. Memorize this once and you'll never write a bad
prompt again.
Part What it answers Example
1. Role Who are you? Who is Claude pretending to
be?
"I'm a small business owner in Lagos. Act
as my marketing advisor."
2. Task What exactly do you need? "Write three Instagram captions for my
new bakery's grand opening."
3. Context What does Claude need to know to do it
well?
"My audience is 25–40 year old women in
Lagos. We sell artisanal bread and
pastries. Tone is warm and a little playful."
4. Format How should the answer look? "Each caption under 150 characters.
Include 3 hashtags. Number them 1, 2, 3."
Bad vs. good — a real example
Bad: "Write me an Instagram caption for my bakery." 
What you'll get: something generic with too many emojis, vaguely about cake, useless.
Good: "I run an artisanal bakery in Lagos. I'm opening a second branch in Ikeja next Saturday. My
audience is 25–40 year old women who care about quality ingredients and Instagram-worthy
presentations. Tone: warm, slightly playful, never salesy. Write three Instagram captions for the
grand opening — each under 150 characters, with 3 relevant hashtags. Make each one distinct:
caption 1 emotional, caption 2 informational, caption 3 a soft call-to-action." 
Same task. Same Claude. Wildly different results.
The single most powerful prompting trick
If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember this:
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 7

Ask Claude to ask you questions before doing the work. This one habit changes
everything. 
When the task is complex, instead of trying to write a perfect prompt, just say:
I want to [your goal]. Before you do anything, ask me 5 questions to make sure you 
understand what I actually need. Don't make assumptions — wait for my answers, then 
proceed.
Claude will come back with five clarifying questions. You answer them. Now Claude has the context.
The work that follows is dramatically better than what you'd have gotten from a one-shot prompt.
This is called a leading prompt. You're asking Claude to think with you, not for you. It works for almost
anything: planning a trip, writing a difficult email, structuring a presentation, applying to a scholarship,
choosing between options.
Other prompting moves that work
"Think step by step"
For anything involving reasoning, math, or multi-step plans — add "think step by step" or "show your
reasoning before giving the final answer." Claude will work through the logic out loud and catch its own
mistakes. Skipping this on complex tasks is the #1 cause of confidently wrong answers.
Show, don't tell
If you want output in a specific style, give Claude an example. "Here's an email I wrote that worked well:
[paste]. Match this tone for my new email about [topic]." This works far better than describing the style in
adjectives.
The "what would change your answer" trick
When Claude gives you advice and you're not sure if it's right, ask: "What information would change
your answer? What are you assuming?" Claude will surface its assumptions, and you'll catch the ones
that don't match your situation.
Ask for the opposite
Got a draft you like? Ask Claude: "What's the strongest argument against this?" or "How would a skeptic
respond?" You'll find weaknesses you missed.
Iterate, don't restart
If the first answer is 70% right, don't open a new chat. Just say: "Good direction, but make it shorter and
drop the formal tone." Conversation context is your friend. Each turn refines the work.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 8

What NOT to do
Don't be vague. "Help me with my email" produces nothing useful. "Help me reply to this email from
a customer asking for a refund" gives Claude something to grip.
Don't pile on too many tasks at once. If you ask for "research, summary, recommendations, and a
draft email," you'll get a shallow version of all four. Do them one at a time.
Don't accept the first answer if it's not right. Push back. Ask for revisions. Claude won't get tired
or take it personally.
Don't be afraid to over-explain. "Too much context" almost never hurts. "Too little context" almost
always does.
A prompt template you can steal forever
When in doubt, fill in this:
I am [who you are].
I am trying to [what you're trying to do].
The audience or context is [who this is for / situation].
Specifically, I need [the exact thing].
Format: [how the answer should look].
Constraints: [anything to avoid; length limits; tone].
Before you start, ask me any clarifying questions if something is unclear.
This single template, filled in honestly, will get you better results than 90% of prompts in the wild.

4. Choosing the right model for the job
When you open Claude, you'll see a model selector. As of mid-2026, you have three main choices.
Picking the right one saves you usage limits and gets you better results.
Model Best for Speed Uses your usage
limit
Haiku Quick questions, simple summaries, classifying or sorting things,
short writing tasks
Very
fast
The least
Sonnet Most things. Writing, research, analysis, drafting documents,
working with files. The everyday choice.
Fast Moderate
Opus Complex reasoning, hard analysis, anything where you need to be
sure the answer is right
Slower The most
The simple rule
Default to Sonnet. It handles 80% of what you'll ever need. Switch up to Opus when you're stuck on a
hard problem and Sonnet's answer doesn't feel right. Switch down to Haiku when you have lots of small
tasks and want speed.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 10

Practical examples
What you're doing Best
model Why
Sorting your emails into "reply now" vs.
"ignore"
Haiku Simple, repetitive classification. Speed matters.
Writing a weekly status report Sonnet Needs writing quality. Doesn't need deep
reasoning.
Drafting an email to a customer Sonnet Same. Default for any writing task.
Reviewing a contract for risks Opus You want it to think carefully and catch subtle
issues.
Researching scholarships and ranking them
by fit
Opus Needs to weigh many factors. Worth the extra
cost.
Generating 50 social media post variants Haiku Volume and speed matter more than depth.
Planning a 5-year career transition Opus Big decision. You want the best reasoning
available.
Practical tip: Start a task on Sonnet. If the answer feels shallow or wrong, don't fight it — switch to
Opus and re-ask. The model dropdown is right there. Switching mid-conversation is fine. 
Which models do you have access to?
Free plan: Haiku and Sonnet. Pro plan ($20/month) and above: all three, plus Cowork. If you're serious
about using Claude regularly, Pro pays for itself in the first week through faster work and less re-do.

5. Projects, files, and connectors
This is the chapter most people skip. Don't. The setup work in this chapter is what makes everything in
Part 2 possible.
Projects: stop re-explaining yourself
If you find yourself starting every chat with "I'm a project coordinator at a small NGO in Port Harcourt,
here's what we do, here's our tone..." — you need a Project.
A Project is a workspace inside Claude where you can:
Write instructions that Claude reads at the start of every chat in that project (your role, your tone
preferences, what to never do).
Upload files Claude can reference forever (style guides, past examples, contact lists, FAQs, brand
guidelines).
Keep all related chats grouped together so you can find them later.
Projects work with both Chat and Cowork — you can start a Chat conversation inside a project or hand
a Cowork task off inside the same project, and Claude uses the same instructions and files either way.
How to create one
1 In Claude (browser, desktop, or mobile), click Projects in the sidebar.
2 Click + New Project. Give it a name like "My Bakery Marketing" or "Job Applications 2026."
3 In the project, find the Instructions field. Write a few paragraphs covering: who you are, what
this project is for, tone preferences, and rules.
4 In the Knowledge section (also called Project Knowledge), upload reference files: examples,
style guides, anything Claude should know.
5 Now start a new chat inside that project. Notice you don't have to explain yourself — Claude
already knows.

What good Project Instructions look like
PROJECT: My Bakery Marketing
I run "Sweet Crumb," an artisanal bakery in Lagos. We have one branch in Lekki and 
are opening a second in Ikeja in May 2026.
WHO MY CUSTOMERS ARE
Mostly women, 25–40, middle to upper income, who care about ingredient quality and 
Instagram-worthy presentation. They follow international food trends and expect us 
to as well.
OUR TONE
Warm and a little playful. Never corporate. Never salesy. We talk like a friend who 
happens to bake well, not like a brand.
THINGS TO ALWAYS DO
- Use British English (we're in Nigeria; "favourite" not "favorite")
- Mention specific ingredients when describing products
- Keep Instagram captions under 150 characters
- Always include relevant hashtags
THINGS TO NEVER DO
- Never use "ZADDY," "fire," or other slang that doesn't fit our brand
- Never make claims about being "the best" or "Lagos's #1"
- Never use more than 2 emojis per caption
Spend 15 minutes on this once. You'll save hours every month.
Files: giving Claude reference material
You can upload files in two places:
In a Project's Knowledge: Files Claude can see in every chat in that project. Use for reference
material that doesn't change often (style guides, past reports, FAQ lists, your CV).
In a single chat: Drop a file directly into the chat box. Use for one-off documents (a contract to
review, a meeting transcript, a customer's CV they sent you).
Claude can read PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, screenshots, plain text files. For most
documents under 30MB, it just works.
Tip: If you have 5 examples of "good emails" you've written before, upload them all to a "My
Communication" project. Now every email Claude drafts for you in that project automatically matches
your voice. 
Connectors: plugging Claude into your apps
This is the magic step. Once Claude can see your actual Gmail, Notion, Calendar, or Drive, the quality
of help jumps dramatically.
• 
• 
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 13

How to add a connector
1 In Claude, click Settings or Customize.
2 Find the Connectors section.
3 Click the app you want. Most useful to start: Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, Google Drive.
4 Sign in to that app and approve the permissions Claude asks for.
5 Done. Claude can now read that app's data when you ask.
How connectors and projects work together: A connector lets Claude reach into your apps. A project
tells Claude how to think about what it finds there. Combine them and Claude becomes powerful: "Read
my Gmail, and write the reply in our brand's tone (which is in the project instructions), referencing our
FAQ document (which is in project knowledge)." 
What to connect first
Don't connect everything on day one. Start with the one app you use most:
If you live in email: Connect Gmail.
If you organize work in Notion: Connect Notion.
If you live in spreadsheets: Connect Google Drive (gets you Sheets and Docs).
If your team is on Slack: Connect Slack.
Privacy note: Connectors only read data when you ask Claude to use them in a specific task. Claude is
not constantly reading your inbox in the background. You can disconnect any app at any time. Don't
paste anything into Claude that you wouldn't email a contractor.

6. Email assistant: daily inbox triage
Need: Gmail connector Time to set up: 15 min Best model: Sonnet
The goal
Every morning, Claude looks at your inbox, tells you what needs your attention, drafts replies for
the urgent ones, and quietly archives the noise. Either you start it manually each morning (Chat),
or it runs on its own at 7:30 AM (Cowork).
Step 1 — Set up a project for your email assistant
Create a project called "Email Assistant." Add instructions like this:
I'm [your name], [your role] at [your organization].
WHO EMAILS ME
- Customers asking about [your products/services]
- Internal team members at [organization]
- Vendors and partners
- Newsletters and promotional content (mostly noise)
MY EMAIL VOICE
[Describe how you write. Formal? Casual? Brief? Warm? Use 2–3 examples.]
WHEN YOU DRAFT REPLIES
- Always create them as drafts, never send automatically
- Match my tone (see examples in project knowledge if I uploaded any)
- Keep replies under 5 sentences unless complexity demands more
- Always end with a clear next step or question
- If a reply requires information I haven't given you, leave a [BRACKETED 
PLACEHOLDER] for me to fill in
DO NOT
- Reply to anything sensitive (legal, HR, financial decisions) — flag those for me 
to handle
- Make commitments on my behalf about prices, deadlines, or scope
Optionally, upload 3–5 examples of emails you've written that you're proud of. This teaches Claude your
voice better than any description.
Step 2 — The Chat version
CHAT  Each morning, open the Email Assistant project. Start a new chat. Paste:
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 15

Look at my Gmail inbox from the past 18 hours. Sort everything into four buckets:
1. REPLY NOW — urgent, waiting on me, will block someone if I don't respond today
2. REPLY TODAY — needs a response but not urgent
3. FYI — no action needed, just for awareness
4. NOISE — newsletters, promotional, automated; safe to archive
For everything in REPLY NOW and REPLY TODAY, draft a reply as a Gmail draft. Match 
my voice (see project instructions). Don't send anything.
At the end, give me a one-paragraph summary: how many in each bucket, and the top 3 
things I should handle first.
Claude reads your inbox, creates drafts in Gmail (which you can review and send with one click), and
gives you the summary. Total time: about 60 seconds. Save you: about 30 minutes of inbox processing.
Step 3 — The Cowork version
COWORK  Switch to Cowork mode in the same project. Give it the same prompt above and set a
schedule. Set:
Frequency: Weekdays
Time: 7:30 AM
Now every weekday morning, before you sit down with coffee, your inbox is already triaged and the
urgent replies are drafted. You wake up, you open Gmail, and your day is half-done before it started.
Because Cowork can run in the cloud, this works even if your laptop is closed — the task runs on
Anthropic's servers and the drafts appear in Gmail whenever you next check.
Variations to try
Add: "Also flag any emails where someone is waiting more than 3 days for a reply from me."
Add: "Search my sent folder for things I committed to do this week. List them as a 'commitments to
honor' section."
Add: "If anyone mentions a meeting request, check my Calendar for free slots and propose 2–3 in
the draft reply."

7. Weekly work reports
Need: Gmail, Calendar, Notion (or your tools) Time to set up: 25 min Best model: Sonnet
The goal
Friday afternoon arrives. Instead of staring at a blank Google Doc trying to remember what you
did this week, your weekly report is already drafted — pulled from your real activity. You spend 5
minutes editing instead of 45 minutes writing.
Step 1 — Project setup
Create a project called "Weekly Report." Instructions:
I'm [name], [role] at [organization].
WHO READS MY WEEKLY REPORT
[My manager / the chairman / my team]. They have less than 3 minutes. Optimize for 
scannability.
MY MAIN PROJECTS THIS QUARTER
- [Project 1 — short description]
- [Project 2 — short description]
- [Project 3 — short description]
WHAT THEY CARE ABOUT
- Outcomes shipped, not activity logged
- Where I'm stuck and need help
- What's coming next week
TONE
Direct. No marketing language. No "synergy" or "leverage." Past tense for completed 
work.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 17

Step 2 — The prompt
Generate my weekly report for the week ending [today's date].
Look at:
- My Gmail SENT folder this week — what did I commit to or follow up on?
- My Google Calendar — what meetings did I attend, and what were the key ones about?
- My Notion pages — what did I create or significantly edit this week?
Produce a markdown report with these sections:
## TL;DR
2 sentences. The headline.
## Wins this week
3–5 bullets. Concrete things shipped or moved forward. Each bullet should answer "so 
what?"
## In progress
Where each main project stands.
## Blockers / asks
Anything I'm waiting on, stuck on, or need help with. Be specific.
## Next week's focus
Top 3 priorities.
## Meetings summary
One line per meeting. Skip the routine ones.
RULES
- If a section has no real content, write "no significant activity" — don't pad.
- Source claims where possible. ("Closed contract with Acme — see email Tuesday")
- Maximum 350 words total.
Step 3 — Chat vs. Cowork
CHAT
Friday afternoon, open the project, start a
chat, paste the prompt. Read the draft. Edit.
Copy into wherever your reports go.
Time: 5–10 minutes total.
COWORK
Switch to Cowork and set the same task to
run on a Weekly, Friday 4:00 PM schedule.
Friday at 4, the report is ready — whether
you're at your desk, on the road, or on your
phone.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 18

Iterate after the first run
The first version probably won't be perfect. Tell Claude what to fix:
"This was too long. Cut to under 250 words next time."
"You missed the SpendRule launch. Make sure to check Notion pages tagged #shipped, not just
edited."
"The tone was too casual. Match my actual past reports — I'll upload three to project knowledge."
By week three, the report is dialed in.

8. Research and compilation
Need: Chat is enough; Drive helpful Time to set up: 5 min
Best model: Opus for synthesis, Sonnet for gathering
The goal
You need to research a topic and produce a structured summary — competitors for a business
plan, scholarship options for grad school, suppliers for a product, learning resources for a new
skill. Claude does the heavy gathering and synthesis; you do the judgment.
The big idea: research is a conversation, not a query
Bad research prompts treat Claude like a search engine. Good ones treat it like a researcher you're
briefing. The difference is iteration.
Step 1 — Brief Claude with a leading prompt
I'm researching [topic]. My goal is [why you're researching it].
Before you do any research, ask me 6 questions to make sure you understand:
- What I already know
- What decision this research will inform
- What "good" looks like in the result
- Any constraints (budget, geography, timeline, credentials)
- What sources or angles I trust or distrust
- What format I want the final output in
Wait for my answers. Don't start searching yet.
Answer Claude's questions honestly. The next answer will be 10x better than if you'd skipped this.
Step 2 — Have Claude make a research plan
Now propose a research plan: what you'll look into, in what order, and how you'll 
structure the final output. Don't search yet — just outline the plan so I can 
approve or adjust.
Approve, adjust, or redirect. Now you and Claude have a shared plan.
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 20

Step 3 — Let Claude do the work
Good. Proceed with the research. As you go, cite sources. Flag anything you're 
uncertain about. If you find conflicting information, list both perspectives instead 
of picking one.
Claude searches the web, reads, synthesizes. You get a structured output instead of a wall of links.
Step 4 — Pressure-test the result
Don't accept the first synthesis. Push:
Now play devil's advocate. What did you miss? What are you most uncertain about? 
What would change your conclusions?
Claude will surface gaps and weak points. Iterate until you're satisfied.
Cowork for bigger research jobs
For a research job that's going to take Claude 20–30 minutes of searching and reading, hand it to
Cowork. Describe what you want, let it plan, approve the plan, and go do something else. Come back to
a completed report. This is especially useful on mobile — kick off a research task from your phone while
you're in a meeting, review the result later.
A real example: researching scholarships
I'm a Nigerian student finishing my undergraduate in computer science. I want to do 
a master's abroad in 2027. Family budget is roughly 5 million naira; anything above 
that needs a scholarship to cover.
Before researching, ask me 6 questions to clarify what I'm looking for.
Claude will probably ask: target countries, field specialization, GPA, GRE/IELTS status, work
experience, citizenship constraints, etc. You answer. Then:
Based on my answers, propose a research plan. What scholarships should we 
investigate, and in what order?
Claude proposes (e.g., Chevening, Commonwealth, DAAD, country-specific, university-specific,
Nigeria-focused like MTN Foundation or PTDF). You approve. Claude researches each, ranks by fit,
surfaces deadlines and requirements. You walk away with a structured shortlist instead of 200 browser
tabs.
Why Opus for the synthesis step: When Claude has to weigh many options against each other, the
deeper reasoning of Opus produces noticeably better recommendations. Switch the model dropdown to
Opus before the synthesis turn. 
Automating with AI · Beginner Edition · Shammah Nei · Page 21

9. Job and scholarship applications
Need: Project with your CV uploaded Time to set up: 20 min
Best model: Sonnet for drafts, Opus for tough essays
The goal
Stop writing every cover letter, statement of purpose, and personal essay from scratch. Set up a
project once with your real history, and Claude tailors each application to the specific opportunity.
Step 1 — Build your "About Me" project
Create a project called "Applications." This is your master file for any job, scholarship, fellowship, or
grant application.
Upload to project knowledge:
Your full CV (the long version, with everything)
Your transcripts if you have them digitally
2–3 essays or cover letters you've written before that you're happy with (Claude learns your voice
from these)
A "stories file" — see below
The stories file (the secret weapon)
Most application essays come down to telling stories. Write a single document called stories.md  that
contains 8–12 of your formative experiences in detail:
## The time I taught my younger sister to code
[3–4 paragraphs of detail. What happened. What you learned. Specific moments.]
## Leading the robotics team in 2024
[Same structure.]
## The startup that failed
[Same structure.]
## Why I care about education access
[Same structure.]
Upload this to project knowledge. Now Claude has a library of your real stories to draw from when

13. Managing your usage and tokens
Every Claude plan has a usage limit. If you ignore it, you'll hit a wall mid-week and have to wait. If you
understand it, you can stretch it indefinitely.
What's a token?
A token is roughly 3/4 of a word in English. When you send a message, Claude counts the tokens in
your message + the conversation history + any uploaded files + project knowledge + Claude's
response. All of it counts.
That last part is important: everything in the conversation history counts every turn. If your chat is
30 messages deep, every new message is processing those 30 messages again. This is why long
chats feel slower and use more of your budget than fresh ones.
Cowork uses more tokens per task than Chat. That's because Cowork can take many steps under
the hood — reading files, taking screenshots, calling connectors, running through plans. A single
Cowork task can burn what would be many Chat messages. Worth it when the task saves you an hour;
not worth it for things a single Chat message could answer. 
Five ways to use less and get more
1. Start a new chat when the topic shifts
Don't keep one mega-thread for everything. When you finish a task, close that chat. Open a new one for
the next thing. You'll get faster, cheaper responses, and Claude won't get confused by unrelated history.
2. Use Projects to avoid re-uploading the same files
If you're uploading your CV and style guide every time you start a new chat, that's tokens you're
spending unnecessarily. Put them in a project once and stop re-explaining.
3. Pick the right model for the task
Using Opus to summarize a 4-line email is like driving a Range Rover to your kitchen. Sonnet handles
80% of work fine; Haiku handles the simplest tasks even cheaper.
4. Be explicit about output length
Claude will write as long as the task seems to warrant. If you say "give me 5 ideas," you'll get more
concise output than if you say "give me ideas." For drafts where you'll edit anyway, ask for shorter.
5. Match the mode to the job
Use Chat for quick things. Use Cowork for multi-step, longer, or repeated work. Sending "what's 2+2" to
Cowork wastes budget; sending "read my inbox, categorize, draft replies, log the results" to Chat means
you're doing the coordination yourself.

14. Common problems and fixes
"The output is generic"
The cause is always the same: Claude doesn't have enough context. Three fixes:
Add who you are, who it's for, and what good looks like to your prompt.
Show examples of past work you're happy with.
Ask Claude to ask you questions before drafting.
"My Cowork task didn't run on schedule"
Two things to check, in order:
Is the task set to run in the cloud, or does it need your desktop? If it needs desktop features (reading
local files, driving your browser), the desktop app has to be open at the scheduled time.
Cloud tasks should just run. If one didn't, check the task history in the Cowork sidebar — you'll
usually see an error explaining why (a connector expired, a permission was revoked, an input file
was missing).
"My connector keeps disconnecting"
OAuth tokens sometimes expire. Go to Settings → Connectors, click the affected app, re-authorize. If it
happens often, the original permissions you approved may have been too narrow — when you re-add,
accept all the scopes Claude requests.
"Claude refused to do what I asked"
Sometimes Claude is over-cautious. Try rephrasing with more context — explain why you need it, who
you are, what you'll use it for. If it's a legitimate task, it'll usually proceed with more context. If it's
something genuinely problematic (drafting deceptive content, bypassing security on something not
yours), that's the safety system working.
"Claude made up something that isn't true"
This is called hallucination. Reduce it by:
Giving Claude the source documents instead of relying on its knowledge.
Adding "If you don't know, say so. Don't guess." to your prompt.
Asking Claude to cite sources for any factual claims.
Pressure-testing answers: "What's your confidence level on each claim? Which would you want me
to verify?"
